explain.title: What is a linear equation?
explain.body: An equation of the form ax + b = 0 where ‘a’ and ‘b’ are constants, a ≠ 0 and ‘x’ is a variable, is called a linear equation in one variable. In linear equation, the highest power of the variable is always 1.

explain.title: How do you solve one?
explain.body: Simplify both sides if needed. Move variable terms to one side and constant terms to the other by adding or subtracting the same terms on both sides. Then divide or multiply by the coefficient of the variable to find its value.

explain.title: Why check the answer?

explain.title: Show the solution on a real line

explain.title: Inequality symbols
explain.body: The four symbols are > (greater than), < (less than), ≥ (greater than or equal to), and ≤ (less than or equal to). Adding or subtracting the same constant on each side, or multiplying or dividing each side by a positive constant, does not change the order. Multiplying or dividing by a negative constant changes the order.

explain.title: One-variable solutions
explain.body: Solve an inequality as you would an equation, but reverse its order if you multiply or divide by a negative constant. A strict inequality has an open endpoint on a real line; an inequality with ≥ or ≤ has a filled endpoint.

explain.title: Half-planes and boundary lines
explain.body: The graph of the corresponding equation is the boundary line. It divides the plane into two half-planes. Use a dashed line for > or < because the boundary is not included, and a solid line for ≥ or ≤ because it is included.

explain.title: Testing a point and graphing a system
explain.body: Choose a point not on the boundary line, usually (0, 0), and substitute its coordinates into the inequality. If it makes the inequality true, shade the side containing that point; otherwise shade the opposite side. For a system, the common shaded region is the solution region.

mistakes: Forgetting to reverse the inequality sign after multiplying or dividing by a negative number.
Drawing a solid boundary for < or >, or a dashed boundary for ≤ or ≥.
Shading a side without testing a point, or shading the opposite side after the test shows the point satisfies the inequality.
Treating a system's solution as either shaded region instead of the common region.
Using a point on the boundary as the test point.

explain.title: Constraints and decision variables
explain.body: While tackling a certain problem from everyday life each linear inequality concerning the problem is named as problem constraint. The system of linear inequalities involved in the problem concerned is called problem constraints. The variables used in the system of linear inequalities relating to the problems of everyday life are non-negative and are called non-negative constraints. These non-negative constraints play an important role for taking decision. So, these variables are called decision variables.

explain.title: Feasible region and feasible solution
explain.body: A region which is restricted to the first quadrant is referred to as a feasible region for the set of given constraints. Each point of the feasible region is called a feasible solution of the system of linear inequalities (or for the set of a given constraints). A point of a solution region where two of its boundary lines intersect, is called a corner point or vertex of the solution region.

explain.title: Objective and optimal solutions
explain.body: A function which is to be maximized or minimized is called an objective function. The feasible solution which maximizes or minimizes the objective function is called the optimal solution.

explain.title: How to find the best value
explain.body: Graph the solution set of linear inequality constraints to determine feasible region. Find the corner points of the feasible region. Evaluate the objective function at each corner point to find the optimal solution.

mistakes: Shading the wrong half-plane: test (0, 0) when it is not on the boundary line.
Forgetting that x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0 restrict the feasible region to the first quadrant.
Using a dashed boundary for ≤ or ≥; these inequalities include their boundary lines.
Missing a corner point, especially the intersection of two boundary lines.
Evaluating the objective function at only some of the corner points.
Giving only the maximum or minimum value without stating the corner point where it occurs.

explain.title: Linear equations
explain.body: A linear equation has an equals sign and a variable of degree 1. Solve it by using inverse operations to isolate the variable. For example, 5x − 10 = 10 gives x = 4.

explain.title: Linear inequalities
explain.body: An inequality uses signs such as <, >, ≤, or ≥. Solve by isolating the variable and keep the inequality direction correct. A strict inequality such as x < 3 does not include 3.

explain.title: Boundary lines and half planes
explain.body: The equation formed from a linear inequality is called the associated equation. Its line divides the plane into two half planes; the inequality tells which side satisfies the condition.

explain.title: Feasible region and vertices
explain.body: The feasible region is the region that satisfies all the constraints. Its corner points are also called vertices.

explain.title: Objective function
explain.body: A function that is to be maximized or minimized is called the objective function. Check its value at each corner point of the feasible region, then choose the greatest value for a maximum or the least for a minimum.

mistakes: Calling a statement with an inequality sign an equation.
Including the endpoint in a strict inequality such as x < 3.
Forgetting to satisfy every constraint when identifying the feasible region.
Mixing up a corner point (x,y) with the value of the objective function at that point.
Giving the maximum or minimum value without stating the corner point where it occurs.
Forgetting to compare the objective function at all feasible corner points.

notes.title: Solving a linear equation in one variable
notes.explanation: A linear equation in one variable has the form ax + b = 0, where a ≠ 0. To solve one, simplify both sides, isolate the variable, and divide or multiply to find its value. For example, 3x − 5 = 7 gives x = 4; and (x − 2)/5 − (x − 4)/2 = 2 gives x = −4/3.
notes.simple: Get the variable by itself, then check that your answer makes the original equation true.

notes.title: Graphing a linear inequality
notes.answer: Use a dashed boundary line and shade the half-plane containing the origin.
notes.explanation: For a linear inequality in two variables, first draw its boundary line. Use a dashed line for < or >, and a solid line for ≤ or ≥. Then test a point not on the line—usually (0, 0)—to decide which side to shade. For a system, shade the solution to each inequality and take the common region. For example, the boundary of x + 2y < 6 is x + 2y = 6, and the origin satisfies the inequality, so shade the side containing the origin.
notes.simple: Draw the edge, test a point, and shade the correct side. A system's answer is where all its shaded regions overlap.
examples: For x + 2y < 6, draw the dashed line x + 2y = 6 and shade the side containing (0, 0).
For x + 2y ≤ 6, draw the solid line x + 2y = 6 and shade the side containing (0, 0), including the line.
steps: Draw its graph as a dashed line because the inequality uses <.
notes.checkQuestion: For x + 2y < 6, should the boundary line be dashed or solid, and which side is shaded?
notes.checkAnswer: Draw a dashed line x + 2y = 6 and shade the side containing (0, 0).

notes.title: Finding the best value at a corner point
notes.answer: The maximum or minimum occurs at a corner point of the feasible region.
notes.explanation: A feasible solution is any point that satisfies every constraint. To find the maximum or minimum of an objective function, find the feasible region, identify its corner points, and evaluate the function at each corner point.
notes.simple: Find the allowed region, check its corners, and see which corner gives the biggest or smallest value.
steps: Graph all the constraints and identify their common feasible region.
Find the corner points of that region.
Substitute each corner point into the objective function.
Compare the values to find the maximum or minimum.
notes.checkQuestion: Where should you evaluate the objective function to find its maximum or minimum?
notes.checkAnswer: A corner point of the feasible region.

notes.explanation: A linear equation has an equals sign and a variable of degree 1. A linear inequality uses an inequality sign. To solve a linear programming problem, find the feasible region, check its corner points in the objective function, and choose the greatest or least value as required.
notes.simple: Solve equations and inequalities using inverse operations. For a maximum or minimum problem, test the corner points of the feasible region in the objective function.
examples: For g(x,y) = x + 4y, the corner point (0,4) gives g(0,4) = 16.
steps: For an equation, use inverse operations to isolate the variable.
For an inequality, isolate the variable and keep the inequality sign in the correct direction.
Use boundary lines and constraints to identify the feasible region.
Find the corner points of the feasible region.
Substitute each corner point into the objective function and compare the values.

written.text: Maximize f(x, y) = 2x + 5y; subject to the constraints 2y − x ≤ 8 ; x − y ≤ 4 ; x ≥ 0; y ≥ 0
modelAnswer: The boundary equations are 2y − x = 8 and x − y = 4.
Their intersection is found from x = y + 4 and 2y − (y + 4) = 8, so y = 12 and x = 16.
The corner points of the feasible region are (0, 0), (4, 0), (0, 4) and (16, 12).
Thus, the maximum is at the corner point (16, 12).
